Prague on foot

Wizzy knows 50 places in Prague, from the big sights to the corners most people walk straight past. Start a walk, put your phone away, and Wizzy taps you on the shoulder when there's something worth looking up at.

The must-sees

  • Charles Bridge

    Bridge · 1402

    Charles IV laid the foundation stone in 1357 and Peter Parler’s workshop built it. Most statues on the parapets today are copies; many originals are kept in the Lapidarium and at Vyšehrad.

    Look for: Under the St John of Nepomuk statue, two bronze reliefs are rubbed shiny by hands. A small cross on the parapet marks where he is said to have been thrown.

  • Church of Our Lady before Týn

    Church

    For two centuries it was the main church of the Hussite reform movement in the Old Town. The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, who worked for Emperor Rudolf II, is buried inside.

    Look for: Tycho Brahe’s red marble tombstone is on a pillar near the altar, showing him in armour.

  • Dancing House

    Building · 1996

    Vlado Milunić and Frank Gehry designed it on a corner left empty by an American air raid in February 1945. Václav Havel, who lived next door, supported the project.

    Look for: On top of the building sits a twisted metal dome nicknamed the Medusa.

  • Josefov (Jewish Quarter)

    Neighbourhood

    It is named after Joseph II, who eased restrictions on Jews in the 1780s. Most of the old ghetto was cleared around 1900, but six synagogues, the Jewish Town Hall and the cemetery survived.

    Look for: On the Jewish Town Hall, the lower clock has Hebrew numbers and its hands turn backwards, as Hebrew reads right to left.

  • National Theatre

    Culture · 1883

    Built with money collected across the country, it burned in 1881 just before full opening and was rebuilt in two years. The words Národ sobě, the nation to itself, are written above the stage.

    Look for: Above the front, bronze goddesses drive chariots pulled by three horses.

  • Old Jewish Cemetery

    Landmark

    Burials took place here from the 15th century until 1787, with graves layered because space was short. Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel, linked to the Golem legend, is buried here.

    Look for: Carvings on the stones tell you about the dead: blessing hands for the Cohen families, a jug for the Levites, animals for family names.

  • Old Town Square

    Square

    A marketplace since the 12th century, it was where 27 leaders of the Bohemian revolt were executed in 1621. Crosses set in the paving by the town hall mark the spot.

    Look for: The Jan Hus monument in the centre was unveiled in 1915, five hundred years after the reformer was burned at the stake.

  • Old-New Synagogue

    Building

    Built around 1270, it is the oldest active synagogue in Europe. Legend says the Golem made by Rabbi Löw still lies in its attic.

    Look for: High on the outside wall, iron rungs climb to the attic door.

  • Prague Astronomical Clock

    Landmark · 1410

    It was installed in 1410 by the clockmaker Mikuláš of Kadaň and is the oldest astronomical clock still working. The calendar dial below was painted by Josef Mánes in the 1860s.

    Look for: Beside the upper dial, Death rings a bell and turns an hourglass, and the Turk beside him shakes his head.

  • Prague Castle

    Palace

    Founded in the 9th century, it has been the seat of Bohemian kings, Holy Roman emperors and now the Czech president. The guard changes at the main gate every hour.

    Look for: At the main gate, two stone giants club and stab their enemies above the guards’ heads.

  • St. Vitus Cathedral

    Church · 1929

    Charles IV began it in 1344 with Matthias of Arras, and Peter Parler continued the work. It was finished only in 1929; the chapel of St Wenceslas guards the door to the crown jewels.

    Look for: In a chapel on the left side of the nave, the stained-glass window was designed by Alfons Mucha.

  • Wenceslas Square

    Square · 1348

    It began as a horse market in the New Town founded by Charles IV in 1348. Huge crowds gathered here in November 1989, during the days of the Velvet Revolution.

    Look for: At the top, Josef Myslbek’s bronze St Wenceslas rides among four Czech patron saints. Praguers meet “under the horse”.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Prague and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Prague passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
